title: Hebrew: Holy Tongue, Daily Tongue
hookLine: the language of Torah and prayer, revived for daily life
carry: hebrew is the holy tongue, spoken again

lines: JUICE, A BUS STOP, A TEXT.
cards: A toddler in Jerusalem tugs at a sleeve and asks for juice. A bus driver calls out the next stop. A teenager types a text and deletes it.
A cashier says have a good day. And on Shabbat morning, a few streets away, a reader stands at a Torah scroll and chants Genesis. Every one of them is speaking Hebrew.
The letters on the scroll are the letters on the bus timetable. The language of the Torah scroll is the language of the grocery list.

teach.b: Ivrit means Hebrew. Turn it four ways. First, the name.
In Genesis, a survivor runs to tell "Abram the Hebrew" that his nephew has been captured: Abram ha-Ivri.

An old midrash plays with the word: ever can mean the other side, and the rabbis picture the whole world on one side and Abraham alone on the other. That's a reading, not a dictionary entry, but it has stuck.
Second, the holy tongue. Tradition calls the Hebrew of the Torah and the prayer book lashon hakodesh.
For a long stretch of history, Jews in many lands spoke other languages at home and in the market: Yiddish, Ladino, Arabic and more.

Hebrew stayed alive in prayer, in study, in letters between scholars, in the blessing over bread. Third, the return. You met Ben-Yehuda, who insisted his family speak Hebrew every day, back in year three.

In modern times a movement set out to speak Hebrew again at the breakfast table, to babies, about the weather. It worked: today it's the daily language of Israel, with words for buses and texting no prophet ever needed.
Fourth, two views side by side.
Some religious communities keep the holy tongue for holy things, praying in Hebrew and talking at home in Yiddish, so prayer words stay set apart.
Others see everyday Hebrew as its own blessing: ordinary life spoken in the language of the Torah.

teach.h: TWO WAYS TO KEEP IT HOLY.
teach.b: Both take the language seriously; they protect it differently.
For the rest of this block, you'll go inside it, letter by letter.

how: Jews pray and read Torah in Hebrew, called the holy tongue; in Israel Hebrew is also the everyday spoken language, while some religious communities keep Hebrew for prayer and study and speak Yiddish at home.

practice: Here is the letter shin: like a cup with three arms rising from a flat base, and a dot above one shoulder, making the sound sh, the first sound of Shabbat and of shalom.
Trace it slowly in the air with your finger, three arms joined at the bottom, and say its sound softly on the out-breath: sh. If you pray, you'll meet this letter in the word shalom.

wordCard.voice: Ivrit. Hebrew: the holy tongue of Torah and prayer, spoken again at the breakfast table. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: Hebrew is the holy tongue, spoken again. The letters of the Torah are the letters of the bus stop. Until tomorrow.
